surface_summary: The Dangerfield Talisman, a valuable family heirloom, disappears from its open cabinet at the Friocksheim estate. Suspicion falls on various guests and family members, with tensions rising as the Talisman mysteriously returns days later. The case appears to be a theft by a left-handed individual with a complex motive.
accepted_facts: The Talisman was missing from its cabinet one morning.
The cabinet doors were found in a state indicating a left-handed person opened it.
A replica of the Talisman was used for display, while the real one was hidden.
Mrs. Caistor Scorton was seen retrieving stolen items from a hiding place.
inferred_conclusions: Eileen Cressage was the thief due to her suspicious night movements.
Eric Dangerfield was the culprit because he was left-handed and had financial troubles.
The Talisman was stolen by an outsider who managed to bypass the alarms.
mechanism_description: The real Dangerfield Talisman was never removed from the estate but hidden in a secret safe deposit behind a panel in the Corinthian’s Room, secured by a mechanical chessboard lock devised by the grandfather. The displayed Talisman was a replica used to maintain the estate’s credit. Mrs. Caistor Scorton, a kleptomaniac, stole the replica and hid it in a hollow tree by the Pool, unaware of the real Talisman’s secret location. The replica was later returned to the cabinet to mislead the guests.
delivery_path: The Corinthian’s Room has a chessboard floor with holes for iron chess pieces.
The grandfather devised a mechanical lock activated by placing knights in a specific sequence.
Behind the tapestry in the room is a secret panel concealing a safe deposit.
The real Talisman and valuable jewels are stored in this secret safe.
Mrs. Caistor Scorton steals the replica Talisman from the cabinet.
She hides the replica and other stolen items in a hollow tree near the Pool.
The Dangerfields and Westenhanger use the chessboard lock to access and recover the real Talisman.
outcome_result: Mrs. Caistor Scorton is revealed as the kleptomaniac who stole the replica, while the real Talisman was safely hidden all along.

false_assumption.statement: The Talisman was stolen by a left-handed thief who had full knowledge of the estate.
false_assumption.why_it_seems_reasonable: The cabinet doors were opened in a way indicating a left-handed person, and Eric Dangerfield, a left-hander with financial troubles, was suspected. The theft coincided with suspicious night movements of several guests.
false_assumption.what_it_hides: The left-handedness clue only applies to the replica theft, not the real Talisman, which was never taken. The real theft was a kleptomaniac stealing the replica without knowledge of the secret safe.

supporting_points: He is left-handed, matching the cabinet door opening.
He had financial difficulties and motive.
He was wandering the house at suspicious times.
He was seen writing a note and paying debts after the theft.
false_solution.the_one_flaw: Old Rollo Dangerfield’s firm assertion that Eric did not take the Talisman and the discovery of the secret safe containing the real Talisman.

red_herrings.description: Eileen Cressage was seen wandering the house at night and switching on her light, suggesting suspicious behavior.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: She was visiting Mrs. Brent to discuss her gambling debts and was cleared by Mrs. Brent’s testimony.

red_herrings.description: Freddie Stickney’s meddling and insinuations caused suspicion to fall on many guests, including himself.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: He was merely an amateur detective with poor evidence and no motive; his presence was disruptive but not criminal.

closed_circle.rationale: Servants were locked out after 11:30 pm, no external entry was possible due to alarms, and all guests were accounted for, leaving only the house guests as possible suspects.

inference_path.observation: The cabinet doors were found with the left-hand door open, indicating a left-handed person opened it.
inference_path.correction: Eileen and Douglas are right-handed; the thief must be left-handed or ambidextrous.
inference_path.effect: Narrows suspect list to left-handed or ambidextrous individuals.
required_evidence: Observation of cabinet door positions in Corinthian’s Room
Eileen’s and Douglas’s hand preference demonstrated by match and cigarette handling

inference_path.observation: Mrs. Caistor Scorton was seen carrying stolen items from a hollow tree near the Pool.
inference_path.correction: She is the one who stole the replica Talisman and other items.
inference_path.effect: Identifies Mrs. Caistor Scorton as the thief of the replica.
required_evidence: Witness statement of Eileen and Westenhanger observing Mrs. Caistor Scorton at the Pool
Physical retrieval of stolen items from tree hollow

inference_path.observation: The real Talisman was missing from the cabinet but later returned.
inference_path.correction: The displayed Talisman was a replica; the real one was hidden in a secret safe.
inference_path.effect: Reveals the theft was of the replica, not the real Talisman.
required_evidence: Discovery of secret safe behind tapestry in Corinthian’s Room
Rollo Dangerfield’s explanation of replica use

inference_path.observation: The chessboard on the floor has holes with plugs and iron chess pieces with spikes.
inference_path.correction: The chessboard acts as a mechanical combination lock for the secret safe.
inference_path.effect: Explains the security mechanism protecting the real Talisman.
required_evidence: Physical examination of chessboard holes and iron pieces
Westenhanger’s reenactment of knight moves on chessboard

inference_path.observation: The leather disc with twine is warped and has been wetted and dried.
inference_path.correction: It is a child’s toy 'sucker' used as a vacuum grip to open the secret panel.
inference_path.effect: Explains how the secret panel is opened without visible handles.
required_evidence: Examination of leather disc and demonstration with water and twine
Westenhanger’s use of disc to open secret panel

inference_path.observation: Mrs. Caistor Scorton’s fingerprints are on the replica Talisman.
inference_path.correction: She stole the replica due to kleptomania, not for financial gain.
inference_path.effect: Confirms her guilt and explains her motive as compulsion.
required_evidence: Mrs. Caistor Scorton’s confession of kleptomania

inference_path.observation: The real Talisman and valuable jewels were found in the secret safe.
inference_path.correction: The Dangerfield Secret was the use of a replica to protect the real Talisman and estate credit.
inference_path.effect: Resolves the mystery and clears innocent suspects.
required_evidence: Recovery of real Talisman and jewels from secret safe
Rollo Dangerfield’s detailed explanation of the Dangerfield Secret

discriminating_test.design: Westenhanger blindfolds Eileen and Douglas separately and asks them to open the cabinet doors naturally. Both open the right-hand door, indicating right-handedness. The left-hand door was found open, indicating a left-handed thief. This test reveals the handedness of the thief without alerting suspects.
discriminating_test.knowledge_revealed: The thief was left-handed or used the left hand to open the cabinet, narrowing the suspect list.
discriminating_test.pass_condition: The test passes if both right-handed participants open the right-hand door, confirming the left-hand door was opened by a left-handed person.

fair_play_explanation: The reader is given detailed accounts of each character’s movements and behaviors, including the left-handedness clue and the presence of a replica Talisman. The mechanical chessboard lock and secret safe are described, allowing the reader to deduce the hiding place. The key observations about Mrs. Caistor Scorton’s behavior and the recovery of stolen items are presented openly. The puzzle is solvable by careful attention to these clues and logical deduction.
